canberra.title: Nickelodeon’s golden franchise returns after nearly 20 years in the wilderness
canberra.snippet: For many kids who grew up in the mid-to-late 2000s, Avatar: The Last Airbender was one of the defining shows of their childhoods. It&#821...
canberra.content:
Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender continues the story of one of the best animated TV shows of the 21st century. Photo: Paramount.

For many kids who grew up in the mid-to-late 2000s, Avatar: The Last Airbender was one of the defining shows of their childhoods.

It’s a contained three-season story about a young boy leading a rebellion against an oppressive nation in a world where people can control elements, called benders.

It won over nearly every person who tuned in, but, aside from a spin-off series in the 2010s that premiered on the Nickelodeon website, the franchise has been lost to time.

Until recently, that is, as Paramount, the parent company of Nickelodeon, released a long-awaited film that serves as a sequel to the original series.

Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender (not to be confused with the name of the original series Avatar: The Last Airbender) is set about a decade after the original series and continues the story of the core five characters: Aang, Katara, Sokka, Toph and Zuko.

After defeating the Fire Nation in the original show, the world is at peace, but while three of the four elemental nations (Fire, Water and Earth) all live in harmony, the massacre of the Air Nomads from the original series still weighs heavily, with Aang being the only person remaining who can control it.

When Aang hears about an ancient ancestor who could grant people the power to control air, he and his friends set out on a journey to learn more about this power and potentially bring his people back from the brink of extinction.

On their journey, they discover a frozen man, Tagah, covered in ancient tattoos similar to Aang’s. Once free, Aang learns about Tagah’s past and his similar quest to bring back airbenders to the world.

The new film had a lot to live up to as the original show is one of the most beloved cartoons of the 21st century, and fortunately, it does for the most part.

Seeing the core group of characters back, albeit aged up, feels like seeing a friend whom you haven’t seen in a long time, and ultimately, that’s one of the movie’s greatest strengths.

The original five characters are so beloved, as each was written so well and given unique arcs that continuing their stories here was always going to be well received.

The animation is also very special. It is quite rare to see hand-drawn animation like this in Western media anymore, which is a shame because modern computer-generated animation loses that personal touch that comes from physically crafted art.

The fights, landscapes and imagery are all top-notch and only build upon the visuals of the original series, which were already fantastic.

The voice acting is also stellar.

While none of the original voice actors returns, the new ones pick up the baton where they left off and continue the legacy. Add in some popular actors like Dave Bautista, Ke Huy Quan and Taika Waititi, and you have an A-list voice cast.

Pity the writing lets it down.

It was always going to be difficult to replicate the arcs and narrative quality of a 60-plus-episode series, where there is time to flesh out characters and story beats.

The issue here is that, with it only being 90 minutes, everything feels more like a side quest than a story that needed to be told. There are decisions within the film that were clearly made to streamline the narrative and manufacture a bit of drama.

While they don’t derail the entire experience, they are a noticeable step down from the tight writing of the original series.

With all that said, it is such a pleasure to be back in this world with the characters I grew up with. It was a unique blast from the past that served as more than just a nostalgia act.

It may not be as good as the show that came before it, but that is more a testament to how awesome that was than to this film being disappointing.

If you loved Avatar: The Last Airbender, you will love Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender.

Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender is now streaming on Paramount+ and showing in select cinemas.

canberra.title: It takes more than a Fix My Street request to tackle Canberra’s illegal dumping epidemic
canberra.snippet: Abandoned mattresses, wooden pallets and rotting rubbish – these are just some of the materials being dumped on Canberra’s ro...
canberra.content:
There have already been more than 2750 reports of illegal dumping to Fix My Street this year. Photo: ACT Government City Services.

Abandoned mattresses, wooden pallets and rotting rubbish – these are just some of the materials being dumped on Canberra’s roadsides and outside homes.

The Fix My Street reporting system has been overhauled in recent years to funnel information to the correct teams, reduce repeat requests for the same job, improve location options so jobs are easier to find, and enhance communication with the person who made the report.

Deputy head Yu-Lan Chan is proud of the improvements so far.

“The operational crews around here have better information now to group things. So there might be a number of tree issues that are reported. Now that operational tree team can go … ‘There’s a couple of [jobs] on the north side, we can group them, we can see this one needs a chipper and this one needs something else’,” she explained.

“They can actually plan all of that and plan it so they just go to one area and do all those jobs in one. Previously, that needed a lot of manual collation.”

Access Canberra is receiving upwards of 45,000 reports across 119 categories.

It’s up to its teams to address these issues, but they’re not sitting around waiting for reports to come in.

Fix My Street requests need to be fitted around their regular duties, including maintaining verges, fixing streetlights, litter picking, cleaning public toilets and mowing and trimming trees (among much, much more).

Place Management director Tessa Roberts said jobs are triaged based on the information provided.

“We will assess it for public safety as the first thing … and then we prioritise it based on what impact it will have on the public,” she explained.

“So if it’s something broken in a public toilet, we know that the public need those facilities, so we’ll go out and do that pretty instantly.

“But if it’s a dumped mattress or whatever that’s in a parkland that isn’t causing a public safety concern, then that would take a bit longer.”

One issue that can get Canberrans’ blood boiling (along with long grass and potholes) is illegal dumping.

There were 2480 Fix My Street requests regarding illegal dumping in 2025 (a 35 per cent increase on 2024), and 1349 of those were considered medium or large dumps.

Already in 2026, there have been 2757 requests.

Members of the public aren’t expected to examine an illegal dump to see if it contains hazardous items, but an eyesore isn’t a reason for teams to go out straight away.

First, the size of the pile will call for different resources.

“We’ve got utes and smaller vehicles … [they] can only pick up a certain amount,” Ms Roberts said.

“Quite often we won’t know what’s in the dump until we’re there doing it.”

Illegal dumping diverts resources away from scheduled work of Access Canberra teams. Photo: ACT Government City Services.

Acting City Presentation executive branch manager Sue Marriage said it wasn’t difficult to pick up an abandoned chair or bag of rubbish, but medium and large loads take much more effort.

“They can often take two people and a truck nearly the whole day to be able to clear all of these illegal dumps and take them to the tip,” she said.

“So those crews that should be out there trimming trees, doing the things that actually beautify the city, we’re instead doing activities like picking up people’s rubbish.”

Illegal dumping’s an especially tough problem for Canberra – and every city – because of the huge diversion of resources.

The government still has to pay the fees to dispose of such material at the tip.

And there’s another reason why dumped rubbish may be left for weeks on end.

“We limit the response to illegal dumping where we can so as not to incentivise it,” Transport, Territory and Municipal Services deputy director-general Bruce Fitzgerald said.

“If people see responsiveness to mattresses dumped by the side of the road, that becomes the default answer as to how you dispose of a mattress, and that would be a significant cost, a diversion of resources that we simply can’t afford.

“So there’s always that balance for us.”

Covert operations are used at hotspots to issue fines, and the ACT has a free bulky waste program (for up to 2 cubic metres of material), but it only had a 10 per cent take-up rate in 2025.

“It’s a great service, but unfortunately, it just hasn’t cut through like we’d like it to,” Mr Fitzgerald said.

“It’s not necessarily that people don’t know that the service is available; it’s often the fact that they’ll go out there, it’s a sunny Saturday morning, and they just want to get rid of something then and there.

“Because we use a bookable service, it might be four to five months before the service actually comes to your door, and so people take the easy way out, which is to dump it.”

Illegal dumping continues to be a problem across Canberra. Photo: ACT Government City Services.

Access Canberra continues to work on ways to improve its systems, streamline processes and ensure jobs can be responded to quickly.

The backlog of Fix My Street requests has reduced from 38,000 open jobs to 18,000 for 2024-25, and the average time to close a job has reduced to 15 days.

One way Canberrans can find out whether an issue is actually part of upcoming works is to check online.

The City Services website now lists the upcoming program for each region.

Despite the work, Canberrans are encouraged to keep letting the teams know what needs to be done.

“There is often a misunderstanding as to what’s been reported and what is causing a risk of harm to the community,” Mr Fitzgerald said.

“If we don’t get reports … there’s no general way for us to pick that up, so we still encourage people to report as they’ve seen issues.”

canberra.title: Man carried out ‘entirely predatory’ assaults on two strangers, court hears
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This story refers to attempted sexual assault. A man who sexually assaulted two women sobbed as he said he had “gr...
canberra.content:
Youssef Rekni leaving court on an earlier occasion. Photo: Albert McKnight.

CONTENT WARNING: This story refers to attempted sexual assault.

A man who sexually assaulted two women sobbed as he said he had “great guilt” and wanted to apologise, a court has heard.

In November 2022, Youssef Rekni came across a woman alone sitting at a bus stop. He pushed her to the ground and assaulted her.

About a year later, in November 2023, he assaulted a different woman he met in Braddon. He drove her home before assaulting her.

Rekni, 46, took the witness box during a sentencing hearing in the ACT Supreme Court on Friday (7 August).

Speaking through an interpreter, Rekni sobbed as he told the court he carried “great guilt” over the offending.

Rekni said he offended at a time when he was drinking alcohol for the first time in his life. He also said he was using cocaine.

He said he was under stress at the time because his wife was ill with cancer and “she used to fight with me on any minor issue” and he would “need to leave the house to get away from that”.

Rekni also said repeatedly that he just had a “desire to touch” the women, for which he was “genuinely remorseful”.

“I know that rape is a serious matter. It was not my intention,” he said.

In cross-examination, the prosecutor asked Rekni about what would happen if he encountered “alcohol, stress and drugs” in the future.

In response, Rekni insisted he wouldn’t offend again.

“No, I won’t do it, because my main concern now … [is] to look after my family.”

He also denied the prosecutor’s suggestion that he was blaming “outside factors” for “your choices” to offend.

The prosecutor called for the court to place weight on how his offending was carried out against vulnerable victims.

She pointed to how one of the victims was alone at night and how he put the other victim’s dog away.

“When the submission was made about the predatory nature, looking at the circumstances in which the offending unfolded, I would press the submission it was entirely predatory in nature,” she said.

She also called for a small part of the sentence to overlap in recognition that there were two “distinct and separate” victims.

The prosecutor said Rekni’s remorse remained a question, saying his repeated claims he only wanted to “touch” the victims were him “trying to move himself away from the seriousness of the offending”.

His defence lawyer told the court that his client wasn’t trying to change his plea ahead of sentencing.

“He’s saying what happened amounts to the offences … He accepts that.

“He’s not answering that way, trying to traverse what ultimately happened … [He is] basically saying, ‘It’s not his character, he didn’t go out to do that.'”

The lawyer said Rekni hadn’t targeted his victims because of their vulnerability.

“There’s no dispute that these victims were in a vulnerable situation, but it’s not suggested that it was a period of grooming where he was able to identify someone who was vulnerable … [and] worked on their vulnerability.”

Justice Jon White SC said Rekni would “inevitably” be given prison time and accepted there was an “opportunistic flavour” in his offending.

The court heard that he spent 49 days in custody over the offending before the hearing. He remains in custody.

Rekni has pleaded guilty to attempting sexual intercourse without consent, committing an act of indecency in the third degree and committing an act of indecency without consent.

Justice White will sentence Rekni at a future date.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on (02) 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on (02) 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on (02) 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call triple zero.

You can also submit an online report about a historical sexual assault allegation for incidents that occurred more than six months ago.

canberra.title: Grown-ups say the darndest things: When adults behave worse than children
canberra.snippet: Poolside signs inform parents it’s their responsibility to supervise their children. Sports field sandwich boards remind parents that it’...
canberra.content:
It’s hard enough to teach kids manners, so when grown-ups let the side down, it’s hard to know what to do. Photo: Unsplash.

Poolside signs inform parents it’s their responsibility to supervise their children. Sports field sandwich boards remind parents that it’s just a game. Every theatre performance begins with simple housekeeping- no food or drink, phones off, no flash photography.

And yet, there’s always the phantom parent who assumes others will babysit their child, inflammatory language bandied about on the sidelines at kids’ sports, and some joker will always manage to disrupt the entire theatre with their own pathological need for attention.

So, what to do when adults behave badly?

If you’re an undercover Muay Thai fighter with intimidating stature and a formidable oak-stained hue, you might simply rip your shirt off and serve up a string of expletives to frighten them off. But we all have our own methods …

Introverts may opt to ignore poor behaviour and make deep eye contact with inanimate objects around them. Extroverts may escalate a situation by addressing the problem directly.

But my question is: Won’t somebody think of the children?

Those little sponges are soaking in everything around them. Consciously and unconsciously, they’re assessing the world around them and deciding daily whether to go down the path of good or evil.

When I’m confronted with adults displaying “bad behaviour”, and kids bearing witness, it can present a real conundrum.

Quotes and platitudes swirl in my head. Do I show my kids how to be an upstander, not a bystander? Am I being the change I want to see in the world? But aren’t I also supposed to show them how to rise above, be the bigger person and turn the other cheek?

Most of the time, I find there’s no need for intervention – maybe just a debrief afterwards.

For example, at a recent school district performance that will remain nameless, I quickly grew weary of the personal shoutouts, poorly timed cheers and, unbelievably, one wolf whistle.

There are 1200+ people in the auditorium and dozens of kids on stage trying to focus on their moment – but sure, now is the time to yell “GO SARAH!”

The collective cringe was thick in the air, and let me tell you – the wolf whistle might have found me testing out my Muay Thai skills if the house lights had revealed its origin.

Admittedly, sometimes I am the problem.

Mummy meltdowns over small things are usually followed by an apology and terms like “window of tolerance”, “empty bucket”, or “perimenopause”.

Of course, most examples of adults exhibiting “bad behaviour” are subjective, easily dismissed or minor irritations. However, sometimes kids witness more serious events which demand a response.

I recall one occasion when I felt forced into action because someone’s safety was at risk.

One day out walking, with my littlies trailing behind on scooters, we came upon what appeared to be a domestic violence incident. A woman, with a baby on her hip and tears streaming down her face, was attempting to flee her irate partner as he chased her down and blocked her path – at one point, prostrating himself in the middle of the road in protest.

Cautiously, I altered our intended path and made myself known as an approaching witness, and thankfully this simple encroachment saw the abuser abandon his efforts.

I offered the victim some wholly inappropriately light-hearted words (to avoid traumatising little ears). We walked her to her car, and I left her with pointed eye contact and the words, “Please stay safe”.

I still think about this incident for a few reasons. But it serves as a poignant example of adults behaving extremely badly and the challenge we face teaching kids to behave when they see adults doing differently – while keeping our response safe and appropriate. And that’s not always easy to gauge.

All adults are role models to our children. Some will set an admirable example, while others will demonstrate how not to behave.

I suppose our job is to help kids decipher which is which – it’s just not always clear how. And how we respond may end up teaching the bigger lesson.

Of course, it would be so much easier if everyone would just heed the signs – watch your kids, cool your boots, sit down and shut up.

But I suppose we’re still learning too …

canberra.title: The end of a family legacy stitched into the fabric of Bungendore
canberra.snippet: Having made the decision to close the doors of the iconic Bungendore business Bungendore Leather and Trading, Wendy and Brian Lake are de...
canberra.content:
Wendy Lake (right) and Brian Lake with long-standing employee Sharon Petterson. Photo: Tenele Conway.

Having made the decision to close the doors of the iconic Bungendore business Bungendore Leather and Trading, Wendy and Brian Lake are determined to do it their own way.

After 35 years in business, and on the back of the recent closure of the landmark business The Woodworks Gallery, it’s a departure that won’t go unnoticed in the small town and one that Wendy and Brian did their best to avoid.

“We were on the market for two years; we were a little surprised it wasn’t snapped up. It’s a great business,” Wendy tells Region.

When it became apparent the business wasn’t going to sell, Wendy and Brian announced a retirement sale which will offer up all the stock at a discounted price until it’s all gone, and the past few days have been hectic with people taking their last chances to secure the premium leatherworks that have been a staple of the town since the early 90s.

“We don’t have a set date that we will close, but we know we won’t be here at Christmas,” Brian explains.

The landmark business has been in operation for 35 years and its departure will be felt. Photo: Bungendore Leather.

Still holding out hope for a last-minute buyer, Wendy and Brian are in the process of planning for their future, which will involve a lot more travel, and as they let go of the trade that they formed their lives around, they are reminded of where it all began.

“It’s a multigenerational business; I learned the skills from my mum Meg, who founded the business in 1969,” shares Brian.

As Brian reminisces about the family trade that saw them open outlets in Narooma, Gold Creek, Belconnen and Woden, as well as Bungendore, it becomes apparent how much of the family’s story is built into the walls of the Bungendore business.

As Brian and Wendy walk through the shop, they are surrounded floor to ceiling with all manner of leather products, from handbags and hats to artworks, floor rugs, jackets and even some Kangaroo scrotums, which are surprisingly good sellers. But if you look a little higher, up towards the rafters, this is where the good stuff hides.

The work of Meg Lake sits proudly above the door in recognition of the family legacy. Photo: Tenele Conway.

The wall above the door is dedicated to Meg’s leatherwork; many of the pieces having been gifted to family and friends have been donated back to Brian and Wendy to form a collection showcasing Meg’s fine skills and the craft that kicked off over 57 years of family business.

Brian lights up when he talks about his parents, who have both now passed, and it’s clear to see the family bond has been integral to not only the success of the business but has shaped their whole lives.

“You know Dad could have done anything; he was a lieutenant colonel in the Australian army, he served in Vietnam, he was an amazing man, and he supported Mum in her leatherwork; they did this together.”

Brian and Wendy have a lot of stock to sell in the retirement sale. Photo: Tenele Conway.

In chatting with Wendy and Brian, it’s easy to see why the business has stood the test of time, and it’s not just about the leather. They radiate a welcoming warmth and generously give out hugs to strangers who have quickly become friends. It’s an ethos that’s felt by those who enter their orbit.

In a quiet moment, Brian talks in a hushed voice, crediting the success of the business to Wendy.

“She’s very savvy when it comes to business. My businesses didn’t take off until I met her, and now that she’s ready to retire, I want her up at the front of the plane, and we’re going to enjoy ourselves. She deserves it.”

Since announcing the retirement sale, a few new potential buyers have surfaced, but the pair aren’t holding their breath just yet, as many have fallen through in the past few years. Brian explains that the business doesn’t hinge on his leatherwork skills, and the majority of the stock is sourced or produced around Australia and through their global networks, all of which would be handed over to a new buyer.

In the coming weeks, if no buyers follow through, Wendy and Brian plan to officially pull it from the market and spend their final months wrapping up a lifetime’s work and connecting with the community that means so much to them.

Bungendore Leather and Trading is located at 44 Ellendon Street, Bungendore and is open seven days a week from 10 am until 4 pm.

Original Article published by Tenele Conway on About Regional.

australia.title: Sydney gardener fined almost $200,000 for removing 287 trees to improve harbourside mansion’s water views
australia.snippet: Local council described incident as ‘worst act of environmental vandalism in Lane Cove history’ Get our breaking news email , free app or...
australia.content:
It began with a gardener being hired to trim grass at a harbourside mansion in Sydney – and escalated to payments being left in a shoe for the unlawful felling of hundreds of native trees in protected bushland.

Now a court has fined Yi Wang $187,500 for his role in organising and carrying out the destruction of 287 trees from council-owned foreshore bushland at Woodford Bay in Longueville in late 2023.

The New South Wales land and environment court justice Rachel Pepper convicted Wang last week for helping to orchestrate the clearing of 1,210 sq metres of land beside a waterfront property on Lucretia Avenue.

Wang pleaded guilty to three offences in relation to the unlawful clearing, which Pepper heard destroyed potential habitat for a range of protected and threatened animals, including powerful owls and microbats. It could take three decades to recover.

The unlawful tree clearing also greatly reduced the natural protection previously afforded to an Aboriginal midden, the court heard.

When it sold in 2014 for $7.6m, real estate agents described the Lucretia Avenue property as an “exclusive waterfront” residence commanding “water views from every room”. It boasted a private beach and was “bordering lush reserves”.

The director of Sydney Garden Home, Wang was hired by the stepdaughter of the owner of the adjacent property to the bushland, Yao Wu, for grass trimming work in November 2023.

The next day, Wu asked Wang to clear trees as well, including on public land.

“This is my back yard,” Wang would later claim Wu repeatedly told him.

Wang then hired casual labourers, including a chainsaw operator, and chopped down and removed trees over a 12-day period. The gardener sent regular updates on the progress of the work to his employer via WeChat and was paid in cash, which was often left in a shoe at the front of the adjacent property for Wang to collect.

Lane Cove council would later call those dozen days “the worst act of environmental vandalism” in the area’s history. The mayor, Scott Bennison, said the “outrageous” act needed to be “prosecuted to the full extent possible”.

In September 2024, the council installed a huge double-sided banner on the site of what it labelled “tree vandalism”, demonstrating its “commitment to obscure” harbour views gained by the destruction of the habitat and pledging it would remain in place until the trees grew back “to a suitable height”.

In addition to the fine and the publication of notices about the case in newspapers, Pepper ordered Wang to pay Lane Cove council’s legal costs.

In a statement, the council said it welcomed the judgment, describing it as “a win for native bushland”.

As it was awaiting the outcome of another matter before the court relating to the same location, the council declined to comment further.

The case first came to light through a tip-off from a member of the public. A council ranger then visited the site the day after the last day of clearing. Council officers discovered no approvals, permits, or consents had been issued for any tree removal and private investigators were engaged.

Recorded interviews from those investigators, as well as CCTV footage and invoices from a nearby dump, which showed Wang and the chainsaw operator disposing of ute loads of branches and vegetation, provided evidence for a timeline of events and facts that Wang did not dispute.

The council commissioned expert reports on the impact of the clearing, including by an arborist, a geologist and a senior archaeologist.

Wang argued his conduct was not reckless but rather negligent at its highest.

Pepper accepted references from his wife, mother and friend that Wang was otherwise a person of good character and was unlikely to reoffend.

The native forest canopy he helped clear had stood since at least 1943 and included an endangered ecological community.

Regeneration of the trees to a comparable ecological condition would probably take 20 to 30 years, a period during which regrowth would be susceptible to pathogens and weed invasion, the court heard.

australia.title: Labor open to ‘sensible amendments’ on gambling reforms, minister says – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Coalition demands NDIS changes focus on fraud, corru...
australia.content:
What we learned, Sunday 9 August

Thanks for joining us today. We’re wrapping up the live news blog. Here’s a reminder of the top stories from today:

  • Labor frontbencher Jenny McAllister says the government still thinks they’ve “broadly got the legislation right” on gambling reform but that they’re open to “sensible amendments” if some come forward;

  • Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young has delivered an ultimatum to the Albanese government over its gambling reform, saying the party will not vote for the proposed legislation as it stands;

  • Two planes have narrowly avoided a collision on the tarmac at Sydney airport this morning as it struggles with staff shortages;

  • The premier of South Australia, Peter Malinauskas has visited Apple’s headquarters and met with outgoing chief executive Tim Cook in the United States.

  • Victoria’s new premier, Ben Carroll, says the state government will boost its funding for public schools before the November election,opening up a pathway for a federal cash injection.

  • New South Wales recorded its first cases of H5 bird flu in two local birds on Saturday, including one found near Wentworth on the Murray-Darling Basin.

Key events

  • 6h ago

    What we learned, Sunday 9 August

  • 6h ago

    Labor open to ‘sensible amendments’ on gambling reforms

  • 8h ago

    Flights being spaced out at Sydney airport after tarmac near-miss incident

  • 9h ago

    Jetstar and Qatar Airways plane involved in near-miss while taxiing at Sydney airport

  • 10h ago

    Wilson raises concerns about gambling ads reaching children

  • 10h ago

    Ben Carroll vows to boost Victoria’s school funding to meet Gonski standards

  • 10h ago

    Labor ‘playing games’ on gambling reforms, Sarah Hanson-Young says

  • 11h ago

    Bird flu detected in inland NSW, on the Murray Darling Basin

  • 11h ago

    Good morning

City2Surf returns to Sydney streets

Today was the annual City2Surf race in Sydney, spanning 14km through the CBD to finish at Bondi beach.

Bendigo’s Andy Buchanan claimed victory in the men’s race:

And Sydney’s Holly Campbell won the women’s race:

Body located during search for swimmer at Wollongong

A man’s body has been located after a search for a missing swimmer near Wollongong today.

About 10.40am on Sunday, emergency services were called to Cliff Road, North Wollongong, after reports the belongings of a swimmer who had not returned from the water had been located.

In a statement, NSW police said officers attached to the Wollongong police district, with assistance from Marine Area Command and Surf Life Saving NSW, attended the scene and commenced a multi-agency search to locate the missing man.

After a search of the nearby water, emergency services located the body of the missing swimmer.

He is yet to be formally identified; however, is believed to be aged 32.

A report will be prepared for the information of the NSW coroner.

Labor open to ‘sensible amendments’ on gambling reforms

Josh Butler

On gambling reforms, minister Jenny McAllister says the government still thinks they’ve “broadly got the legislation right” but that they’re open to “sensible amendments” if some come forward.

It’s understood the government is open to making some changes to wagering inducements, after focus on that issue during explosive Senate hearings last week, but that amending some of the advertising frequency rules is less likely at this stage.

McAllister, speaking to News24, said the government’s current proposals are “really significant” and would “make a real difference”.

We want to see this through the parliament.

McAllister said communications minister, Anika Wells, was “very engaged” on the issue and had been “paying attention to the evidence” from last week’s Senate hearings.

Josh Butler

Labor to address ‘exploitation and rorts’ in migration

The NDIS minister, Jenny McAllister, concedes there is “more work to be done” on Australia’s immigration system, saying it was important for people to have “confidence” about how the government was managing intake of new arrivals.

The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, is expected to detail changes to the immigration system at some point in the coming fortnight, after his National Press Club speech was postponed last week. McAllister told News24 this morning that the government was focused on improving the skilled migration system.

“It’s really important that Australians have confidence that the migration system is working in Australia’s interest, and that has been the focus of all our work since coming to government,” she said.

Guardian Australia understands Burke’s changes will probably not include major cuts to intake, and may focus more on integrity measures, targeting people overstaying their visa periods, and those appealing against the end of their bridging visas.

McAllister said Labor wanted to “stamp out exploitation and rorts. We’ve taken steps already to do that, but of course, there’s more to do.”

SA premier pens deal with ChatGPT developer on US trip

The premier who led Australia’s world-first social media ban has signed a landmark artificial intelligence agreement as he courts big tech, AAP reports.

While touring the US, South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas visited OpenAI’s headquarters in San Francisco where he signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with its co-founder and president Greg Brockman.

OpenAI is the developer of ChatGPT, the world’s most popular generative AI chatbot.

It is believed to be the first time an Australian state or territory government has inked an MoU with a major AI company.

The agreement will provide opportunities to develop AI skills, accelerate local research and innovation, attract global investment and spread the benefits of AI across South Australia, Malinauskas said.

In a statement, the South Australian premier said:

We want to lead with ambition and care.

Any initiative taken forward will be human-led and subject to the legal, privacy, security and procurement safeguards South Australians expect

Air safety bureau launches investigation into near collision on Sydney airport tarmac

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) has launched an investigation into the near miss involving a Jetstar and a Qatar Airways plane on the Sydney airport tarmac this morning.

A Jetstar A320 was taxiing prior to a flight to Gold Coast airport when its flight crew observed a Qatar Airways Boeing 777, under tow from an aircraft tug, in close proximity on a crossing taxiway, the ATSB said

In a statement, the bureau said:

Both aircraft were stopped abruptly. A cabin crew member aboard the A320 was injured, and there was damage to the connection between the 777 nose gear and aircraft tug.

The ATSB will collect available data from both aircraft, and air traffic control.

Air safety investigators will interview the flight crew involved, tug operators, air traffic controllers and witnesses, the statement said. CCTV footage will also be collected.

The ATSB requested that anyone with video footage of the occurrence or its aftermath contact the bureau.

Minns describes Sydney airport delays this weekend as a ‘blip’

The NSW premier, Chris Minns, was asked today whether he had spoken to the federal infrastructure and transport minister, Catherine King, about traffic control issues at Sydney airport.

Minns said he had not spoken to King directly, but his team was in contact with the commonwealth about the issue:

Obviously we’ve had an incredibly strong record when it comes to safety in our airports, which you need in a big country … a big wealthy country like Australia, but you know we can’t have massive delays or near misses because it’s just too important for Sydney.

Asked about delays at Sydney airport this weekend, Minns said it was a “a blip that we want to see fixed as soon as possible.”

Josh Butler

Shadow treasurer flags spending cuts to pay for proposed tax measures

Circling back to the shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, on News 24, he pledged there would be spending offsets – read, cuts – to pay for the tax cuts the Coalition has promised, with more details to be released “in good time”.

News24 host Andrew Clennell asked Wilson about the Coalition’s tax policy, saying “your income tax cuts or all your measures are put at up to $110bn over the forward estimates. How are you going to pay for that if you’re elected?”

Wilson didn’t dispute the $110bn figure, replying: “We’re going to make sure that we have offsets, and we’ve said that and we’ll release those in good time”.

We’ve announced, when we’ve announced measures before, offsets and we’ll continue to do so. We’re going through that work right now to make sure that we get best value for the Australian taxpayer because we want to have the incentives in place to grow the economy, to give Australians hope, to look at a future horizon where they believe that hard work’s going to pay off.

Wilson also said the Coalition would seek to “go back and address the systemic issues of corruption that exist at the heart of this government”, after earlier calling for more attention on fraud and corruption issues he claimed existed in the NDIS.

Minns ‘concerned’ by Sydney airport near-miss incident

The NSW premier, Chris Minns, says he is “concerned” to hear about the near miss incident involving a Jetstar and Qatar Airways plane while taxiing at Sydney airport this morning.

Passengers travelling through Sydney airport have been warned of delays this week due to air traffic controller rostering issues.

Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Minns said he was concerned about potential safety risks and stressed the importance of the airport operating at full capacity:

That’s hugely important for our economy.

We’re hopeful that there’s a plan in place to recruit more people for a highly specialised but very important job … we’re opening a brand new airport in the not too distant future, so there’ll be even more strain on that service than there is today. I know it’s hard to employ people, particularly for these specialised services, because we’ve got a very tight labour market. But this isn’t a nice to have; it’s a must have.

Flights being spaced out at Sydney airport after tarmac near-miss incident

AirServices Australia says departures have been spaced out at Sydney airport after the incident involving a Jetstar and Qatar Airways plane this morning.

In a statement, a spokesperson for AirServices Australia said:

Airservices Australia has enacted Air Traffic Flow Management (ATFM) measures including departure spacing at Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport to safely manage projected airborne and departure demands following a reported safety incident between two aircraft moving on taxiways.

We are working with airlines to reduce delays and the impact on passenger travel as much as possible.

Airservices is reviewing the incident and will assist with any safety investigation.

Witness describes Jetstar-Qatar near miss at Sydney airport

A witness to the near miss between Jetstar and Qatar Airways planes at Sydney airport has spoken to the ABC.

Dani Brown was on another plane at the Sydney airport tarmac when she witnessed the incident this morning. She told the ABC the plane’s pilot told passengers there was a “traffic congestion issue”:

It was looking like a very close near miss.

Our flight was meant to leave at 7.15 and we just sat at the tarmac at our gate, because it was quite close to the gate. And we just had to wait until the Jetstar plane was towed away and it was clear for us to move. It was a pretty empty flight for us.

Protective services officers to be stationed at major Victorian hospitals under Coalition plan

The Victorian Coalition has pledged to deploy protective services officers (PSOs) to the state’s major hospitals if it wins November’s state election.

The proposal, unveiled on Sunday, aims to reduce violence at hospitals.

In a statement, the Coalition said 70 PSOs would be deployed as part of a two-year pilot at seven major Victorian hospitals.

PSO teams would provide additional security, respond to serious incidents and escort hospital workers to their vehicles, a statement said.

The opposition leader, Jess Wilson, said:

Doctors, nurses, and healthcare staff should be able to do their jobs safely so that they can provide Victorians with the care they need.

The state’s shadow health minister, Georgie Crozier, said health workers need “greater protection.”

The safety of our health workers is paramount – you should feel safe, feel protected, whether you are triaging a patient in ED or walking to your car after ending your shift.

Man charged over alleged Coogee assault

A man has been charged over an alleged assault in Sydney’s east overnight.

At about 11pm on Saturday, emergency services responded to reports of an assault on Coogee Bay Road, Coogee.

A 26-year-old man was arrested at the scene and charged with assault occasioning actual bodily harm, NSW police said.

Paramedics treated a 41-year-old man at location before he was taken to Prince of Wales hospital, a NSW police statement said.

The 26-year-old man was refused bail to appear before the bail division court today.

Jetstar and Qatar Airways plane involved in near-miss while taxiing at Sydney airport

A Jetstar pilot was forced to brake suddenly when a Qatar Airways plane came into “close proximity” while the other plane was taxiing at Sydney airport this morning.

Guardian Australia understands a Jetstar cabin crew member was injured in the incident, and was treated by paramedics.

The Jetstar flight from Sydney to the Gold Coast was taxiing out from its bay at Sydney airport this morning when the incident occurred.

A Jetstar spokesperson said:

Our aircraft was following instructions by Air Traffic Control when the pilots were forced to brake firmly after another aircraft came in close proximity.

We have commenced an investigation into the incident.

australia.title: Labor open to ‘sensible amendments’ to gambling laws after inquiry hears alcohol and cocaine offered to punters
australia.snippet: Sources say Albanese government willing to tighten rules on betting inducements but less likely to budge on TV and online advertisements ...
australia.content:
The Albanese government is prepared to tighten rules on gambling inducements, but is less likely to budge on advertising rules, as negotiations continue on wagering legislation, which so far has lacked the support needed to pass parliament.

Federal Labor is open to considering amendments to its legislation from the Coalition when MPs return to Canberra this week, sources say.

The government was prepared to make changes around wagering inducements – a focus of explosive parliamentary hearings last week – as part of negotiations, but was less open to tweaking proposed rules on the frequency of advertisements on TV and online.

Additional restrictions on ads are a major demand of gambling harm advocates and the Senate crossbench.

Upper house hearings have aired sensational allegations that wagering companies provided illegal drugs and access to sex workers to keep problem gamblers betting. Betting giants Sportsbet and Tabcorp say there is no evidence to substantiate these claims.

“If the government’s now willing to move on some things, well, good, but the devil is going to be in the detail,” the Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young, a vocal proponent of stronger action, told the ABC on Sunday. “Inducements, of course … should be gone.”

The Coalition, crossbenchers and the Greens have opposed Labor’s reforms as proposed by the communications minister, Anika Wells, meaning the legislation is unlikely to pass in its current form.

Sources said the government was more inclined to deal with the Coalition and would await amendments from the opposition after its party room met in the nation’s capital this week.

The government frontbencher Jenny McAllister said on Sunday that Wells was in discussion with the Coalition and had been “paying attention” to evidence from the recent parliamentary hearings.

McAllister said Labor thought it had “broadly got the legislation right” but was open to “sensible amendments”. “We want to see this through the parliament,” she said.

Inducements can include perks like “bonus bets”, promotional odds, rebates or more VIP enticements like hospitality at events.

The landmark gambling reform report from late Labor MP Peta Murphy called for a total and immediate ban on inducements and their advertising. That issue has been a key focus for advocates within the Coalition, crossbench and Greens – and even among some Labor MPs who want the government to go further.

Gambling companies have opposed changes to inducements.

Hanson-Young, speaking on the Insiders program, suggested she would support the proposed “opt-out” model for online advertising being switched to “opt-in”.

Critics have argued streaming platforms would be able to show more ads during breaks in play under Labor’s current plan if they implemented a “triple lock” function including an opt-out feature. Campaigners have also criticised the legislation for allowing three TV ads per hour from 6am to 8.30pm, with a ban during live sport.

Wells has previously said the government believes the current proposal strikes the correct “balance” between addressing problem gambling while not unduly penalising media companies and sporting codes which rely on wagering revenue.

Labor MP Jerome Laxale last week said he would welcome Labor’s draft laws “being strengthened in the Senate”. The deputy opposition leader, Jane Hume, said the shadow communications minister, Sarah Henderson, was negotiating for new controls over inducements.

Tim Wilson, the shadow treasurer, told News24 on Sunday that the Coalition wanted more action to protect children.

“Under the government’s proposed bill, it doesn’t limit the capacity to advertise to children, and that’s something that I’m concerned about, making sure that we’ve got the measures that are consistent, appropriate, and also reflecting the changing nature of technology,” he said.

Last week’s inquiry heard evidence that gambling ads were being played on Spotify between Disney songs for children.

Hanson-Young on Sunday demanded tougher regulation from the government and stated: “If you are not prepared to do what’s needed here, well, we’ll take this out of your hands and we’ll do it in the Senate ourselves.”

australia.title: ‘Not enough air traffic controllers’: safety concerns at Sydney airport after Jetstar and Qatar planes involved in near-miss
australia.snippet: Planes narrowly avoid collision on tarmac with Jetstar A320 forced to ‘brake firmly’ as Qatar Boeing 777 towed into its path Follow our A...
australia.content:
Two planes have narrowly avoided a collision on the tarmac of Australia’s busiest airport as it struggles with staff shortages.

The Jetstar and Qatar Airways planes almost collided at Sydney airport at 7am on Sunday.

A Jetstar spokesperson said its plane was following instructions from air traffic control when the pilots were forced to brake “firmly” when another aircraft came into “close proximity”. “We have commenced an investigation into the incident,” they said.

Initial inquiries suggested the tug vehicle pulling the Qatar aircraft may not have followed instructions, a source said.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) said it was investigating the “near collision”.

“As reported to the ATSB, a Jetstar A320 was taxiing prior to a planned flight to Gold Coast airport when its flight crew observed a Qatar Airways Boeing 777, under tow from an aircraft tug, in close proximity on a crossing taxiway,” the safety bureau said.

“Both aircraft were stopped abruptly. A cabin crew member aboard the A320 was injured, and there was damage to the connection between the 777 nose gear and the aircraft tug.”

Investigators would interview flight crew, tug operators and air traffic controllers, plus other witnesses, and review any CCTV footage, the bureau said.

Airservices Australia said it was working to safely manage demand at the airport “following a reported safety incident between two aircraft moving on taxiways”.

“We are working with airlines to reduce delays and the impact on passenger travel as much as possible,” a spokesperson said on Sunday. “Airservices is reviewing the incident and will assist with any safety investigation.”

Jetstar flight JQ402 was taxiing on the tarmac when the near-miss occurred. The incident left one crew member needing medical attention at the scene, Jetstar said. No passengers were injured.

The flight was cancelled and passengers re-booked on later services.

The incident came after delays to more than 150 flights passing through Sydney on Saturday as the airport struggled with staffing shortages.

A spokesperson for the airport said Airservices Australia, which oversees air traffic control, was managing reduced air traffic movements. Flights across the network would be affected and delays were expected, the airport spokesperson said.

Airservices Australia had been unable to roster enough staff for three consecutive days, the Airlines for Australia and New Zealand chief executive, Stephen Beckett, told the ABC this weekend.

Beckett called on Airservices to identify the root cause of the issue and detail plans to address it.

Two weeks ago, another near-miss involving two Qantas planes occurred at Sydney airport. The ATSB is investigating the 27 July incident when a Qantas flight was cleared to cross a runway in front of one of the airline’s other planes that had just landed.

Both Qantas planes were cleared to proceed following instructions from air traffic control, a Qantas spokesperson said.

Air traffic control detected the “conflict” and alerted both crews, the ATSB said.

Speaking about Sunday’s near-miss, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, said he was “obviously concerned”.

“Not just the safety risks but we want to make sure the airport is operating at full capacity,” he told reporters.

“That’s hugely important for our economy. We don’t want to see people disrupted if they go to the airport and services are cancelled because there are not enough air traffic controllers.”

Minns said the government was “hopeful that there’s a plan in place to recruit more people for a highly specialised but very important job”.

“We’re opening a brand new [western Sydney] airport in the not too distant future, so there’ll be even more strain on that service than there is today. It’s hard to employ people, particularly for these specialised services, because we’ve got a very tight labour market, but this isn’t a nice-to-have; it’s a must-have. It’scrucial for public safety and our economy.”

Sydney airport faced significant delays on Friday with some passengers forced to sit on the tarmac for more than an hour as more than 120 flights were delayed.

Qatar Airways was contacted for comment on Sunday.

australia.title: Breakfast of champions: Australia’s best porridge makers cause a stir at inaugural national competition
australia.snippet: On Saturday, a sold-out crowd cheered on as 15 contestants battled it out to claim the championship spurtle – with a pinch of Celtic salt...
australia.content:
Oatmeal sloshes out of pots and into stovetop flames as contestants frantically fumble with their finishing touches. The timer is ticking down but spectators clap and cheer, their whoops ringing through the rafters of Pearl Beach memorial community hall before a voice cuts through the chaos: “please make way for the porridge carriers”.

The five cooks step back, glance at each other’s mess, and hope they’ve done enough.

This is the first heat of Australia’s inaugural porridge-making championship.

For 32 years, Carrbridge in Scotland – approximately 17,000km away – has been home to the world porridge-making championship, called the Golden Spurtle.

But the competition has received renewed international attention thanks in part to the 2025 documentary The Golden Spurtle, directed by Australian Constantine Costi, which follows a cast of eccentric yet passionate competitors at the 2023 contest.

While watching the film, Pearl Beach local Mark Gibbins noticed similarities between his hamlet on the NSW central coast and the Scottish town. After a wine-heavy dinner with friends, the Australian competition was born.

“I didn’t think anyone would turn up,” Gibbins says on competition day on Saturday, as he scans the packed hall.

  • Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads

Audience tickets sold out almost two weeks before the event, with some spectators making the two-hour drive from Sydney, while merchandise like shirts and spurtles were wiped before midday.

Named after its seaside location and the specialty implement used to stir oatmeal, the Pearly Spurtle is a celebration of all things Scottish and porridge.

There are 15 competitors vying for the title of Australia’s first porridge champion. They are split into three heats, to compete five at a time.

Modelled after the Golden Spurtle, competitors are given 30 minutes during each heat to cook a litre of traditional porridge, made solely from untreated oats, water and salt – rolled oats and milk are strictly prohibited – and a “creative” porridge, where they can show their flair by making almost any dish that includes oatmeal or oat flour as a key ingredient.

The dishes are blind-tasted by three judges – judge Caroline Velik, who competed in last year’s Golden Spurtle, says she wants a traditional porridge that is thoroughly cooked without being gluggy, and seasoned with “a good amount of salt, but not too much”. The top five contestants then compete in a 30-minute final, where they must make the traditional porridge again.

Whoever reigns supreme will be flown to Scotland to represent Australia at the Golden Spurtle in October.

Though most competitors come from Pearl Beach and can point out their houses from the memorial hall, some have flown from as far as Melbourne to compete.

Semi-retired teacher Paul Woods now lives in Sydney, but he grew up in England, where his father would make porridge for him every winter.

While he’s made porridge for his wife, kids and grandchild, the Pearly Spurtle is a completely different arena.

“I’m a bit nervous,” he says.

“I haven’t really got a competitive bone in my body, and I’m not very sporty.”

All three generations of his family are in the audience holding up hastily made posters proclaiming “pappou’s porridge is so nice, you have it twice”.

But for local Phil Scarf, competition is the name of the game, and there is no one he wants to beat more than his adult daughter, Liz.

“He signed us both up,” she says. “This is just one instance in 36 years of us taking very wholesome family activities and ruining them by making them competitive – that is what we do best.”

Ahead of her heat, Rachel Visontay is feeling apprehensive about her creative porridge. She’s discovered two other contestants’ recipes, like hers, feature figs. “That’s shaken me,” she says.

At the Pearly Spurtle opening ceremony, the City of Gosford pipe band, dressed in tartan and knee-high socks, blasts a bagpipe rendition of Waltzing Matilda as competitors, organisers and kilt-wearers of all ages join a parade around the Pearl Beach community hall.

As the heats begin, the crowd quickly files inside.

Some contestants have trained for weeks, but Sam Vincent is widely considered the one to beat.

Hailing from London, Vincent is a recipe developer for MasterChef Australia and The Great Australian Bake Off, and when the MC reveals his credentials , the audience let out a collective “oooh” and flock towards his station.

But his path to the competition has been fraught after he was forced to pay an $85 luggage check-in fee for his overweight bag of oats.

“They overcharged me big time, so I thought, ‘I’ll show you’,” he says.

During the heat, Vincent frantically hand whips cream, rolls out coconut-and-oat-infused brittle and tosses caramelised pineapples, while tasting every component on the back of his hand. With seconds to spare, he adds a tiny umbrella and a cherry to finish off his pina colada porridge.

A few burners away, former cafe owner Robert Reid is sieving his porridge over a ricotta cannoli filling for his specialty dish. His kilt-clad family whisper with concern as he lifts a patch of burnt tuile from the pan.

After handing in his entry, screenwriter John Collee has the horrifying revelation that he is missing a third of his dish.

“I forgot the salt in the traditional,” he says.

Hours later, after all three heats have concluded, the judges announce the finalists: Visontay, Reid, Vincent, Phil Scarf, and beloved local Muriel Petersen.

They have an hour to prepare for the next stage as Velik entertains the audience with a demonstration of the porridge jaffle that won her the 2025 Golden Spurtle specialty dish category.

But before long, the finals begin and a hush descends over the hall.

Petersen exudes confidence, stirring her porridge one-handed without holding on to the pot handle.

Scarf tells the audience he stirs anti-clockwise every few strokes, contrary to Scottish folklore which advises porridge makers only stir clockwise lest they let the devil into their oats.

Most contestants finish well before the deadline, with Reid worrying the extra time may have led him to overthink his technique.

But Vincent, who spends most of the heat waiting for his oats to cook and joining other contestants in sampling each other’s porridge, pushes it to the last second.

After the final bell rings, the judges head to their porridge conclave to convene.

They emerge 20 minutes later to announce the results. Despite Visontay’s concerns , her creative entry takes out the category’s $500 cash prize, which she says she will spend on more figs.

The traditional heat was much tighter, the judges say, but Reid, with his specialty mix of regular salt and Celtic sea salt, wins the award.

The overall winner of the Pearly Spurtle was also a close call.

But Reid emerges as Australia’s first national porridge champion, booking himself a spot at the world championships.

The judges present him with a mounted spurtle, which he holds over his head as the crowd race over to offer their congratulations.

“We were meant to do a family road trip up the east coast of Australia for all of October, but I guess we’ll go to Scotland instead,” he says.

As organisers pack up banners and trestle tables, they begin discussing plans for next year’s Pearly Spurtle, and float a two-day competition, given the immense popularity of the inaugural event.

“We’re living in this complicated world with complicated things happening,” Gibbins says.

“But this has just resonated with a lot of people who have bought into the simplicity and retro aspects of the humble oat.”

world.title: Spain to introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy
world.snippet: Move comes in response to Rome imposing similar measures after mass migration rush to Ceuta Spain has announced it will introduce tempora...
world.content:
Spain has announced it will introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy in response to Rome imposing similar measures after a mass rush of people from Morocco into Ceuta.

The checks, which come “amid the persistent irregular migration pressure” facing Italy, will start at midnight on Saturday and last until 7 September, Spain’s interior ministry said in a statement.

Hours earlier, Spain threatened Italy with countermeasures if it did not swiftly lift its own border checks, drawing a rebuff from Rome.

The rare spat between the EU and Nato allies came after tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco to Spain’s north African territory on 30-31 July in an unprecedented, deadly rush.

The scenes infuriated EU members that back a hard line on irregular immigration, including Italy, which imposed border checks on people arriving from Spain for one month.

The Spanish government criticised the measure on Friday as “unfair, contrary to the EU’s interests and discriminatory for the Spanish population”.

Foreign minister José Manuel Albares described it as “a torpedo fired at the hull of European unity”.

“We urge the government of Italy to rectify, put an end to the checks and treat Spaniards like other European citizens,” he added.

He threatened “proportional measures” in response by Sunday if Italy failed to comply.

Within hours, the government of Italy’s far-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said it “had no intention of revising the decision” before 15 August, when it said Spanish authorities “expected a new wave of migration” to hit Ceuta.

Meloni’s office said in a statement: “Italy does not accept ultimatums or impositions from abroad regarding national security and border control.

“Only when there is certainty that there are no security or terrorism risks to Italy, that no new wave is occurring, and that no irregular migrants are heading toward European territory, will the decision be reconsidered.”

Spain’s interior ministry announced the reciprocal measures within hours.

Spanish police have been monitoring online rumours and social media about possible fresh arrivals in Ceuta in mid-August, according to local media. But authorities have not expressly said they expect a repeat of last week’s rush.

Border authorities would in the meantime “do their utmost to ensure maximum ease of movement for Spanish and European citizens” who are not affected by border checks, the Italian statement added.

Italy, which does not share a land border with Spain, introduced border controls at maritime and air entry points for third-country nationals arriving from Spain.

The move, announced on 31 July, was an “extraordinary measure” intended to “safeguard national security and prevent possible repercussions for our nation”, Meloni said at the time.

She was among several EU leaders who called for Spain to be suspended from the visa-free Schengen travel zone after the Ceuta incident, despite such a move being legally impossible.

Italy’s coalition government has sought to stop the tens of thousands of people who land in small boats on the country’s shores each year.

The Spanish government warned against “creating rifts and sterile conflicts driven by internal electoral motives” and said “we trust that pro-European sentiment, common sense and good faith prevail”.

Of the 72,000 people who entered Ceuta, 70,000 have returned to Morocco, according to official Spanish figures.

Spanish authorities said 80 people died in the crossings.

Moroccan rights groups, however, estimate the figure to be higher. The Moroccan Association for Human Rights and the European Coordination for Human Rights in Morocco on Friday said at least 141 deaths were recorded and that the toll was likely to rise.

Morocco’s interior ministry has said 11 people died on its side of the border, all but one by drowning.

Those who remain in Ceuta – including hundreds of unaccompanied children – face dire living conditions with little access to food, water and shelter.

world.title: Judge approves Trump effort to end South Sudan TPS protections
world.snippet: Decision follows supreme court ruling that allowed US government to strip protections for Haitians and Syrians Temporary protected status...
world.content:
Temporary protected status (TPS) for hundreds of South Sudanese nationals in the United States is set to end after a federal judge ruled that the Trump administration can move forward with stripping their protections.

On Friday, US district judge Patti Saris of the district of Massachusetts rejected an attempt by immigrant rights organizations including the New York-based African Communities Together to keep TPS for South Sudanese nationals living in the US.

Saris’s decision follows a 6-3 supreme court ruling in June allowing the Trump administration to strip hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians of TPS, which granted them permission to work and live legally in the US.

The supreme court’s conservative majority overturned lower court rulings in New York and Washington DC, which had blocked the administration from ending TPS for more than 350,000 Haitians and about 6,100 Syrians.

A TPS designation allows eligible people from certain countries facing crises including civil war and environmental disasters to remain in the US temporarily, protects them from deportation and allows them to work legally.

In her 15-page ruling, Saris wrote that “as a logical matter, plaintiffs’ arguments rest upon a self-contradictory, self-defeating foundation”.

According to Saris, the plaintiffs’ argument undermined itself, because if the homeland security department (DHS) lacked the authority to terminate South Sudan’s TPS designation, it also would have lacked the authority to issue the designation initially.

“South Sudan’s original TPS designation would thus be invalid by the same token as its termination,” Saris wrote.

In response to the ruling, James Percival, a DHS general counsel said on X: “Every other TPS judge must do the same! Every day these ‘administrative stays’ are in effect is a day the American people are denied what they voted for.”

The Guardian has contacted African Communities Together for comment.

Meanwhile, in a statement on Friday, the immigrant advocacy organization Global Refuge condemned the ruling. The CEO, Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, said: “The reality of the situation is that South Sudan is on the brink of a return to an all-out-civil war. Roughly two-thirds of the population, some 10 million people, now depend on humanitarian aid to survive.

“With only several hundred South Sudanese holding TPS in the US right now, this isn’t a policy forced by scale or strain on our system. To the contrary, this is the administration’s deliberate choice to send a small group of vulnerable individuals and families back into a country where civilians are bearing the brunt of intensifying violence and displacement,” Vignarajah added.

The Trump administration’s effort to strip TPS protections from hundreds of thousands of immigrants comes despite the US government’s own highest-level travel warnings for Americans to several countries affected, including South Sudan, Haiti and Syria.

In the case of South Sudan, the country has been ravaged by years of civil war and political instability that have displaced millions. Since gaining independence in 2011, more than 400,000 people have been killed in conflict, with fighting and ethnic violence continuing to claim civilian lives.

The DHS moved in November to terminate TPS for South Sudan, saying the country ‌no longer met the conditions for the designation, which was first issued in 2011. The department’s action would have led to the end of protections for more than 232 South Sudanese and at least 73 South Sudanese with pending applications. An earlier order by Saris had blocked that from happening.

After the supreme court’s ruling, lawyers for a group of South Sudanese nationals and the non-profit African Communities Together urged Saris to once again block the ‌end of TPS on new grounds that the justices had not addressed.

That included an argument that the DHS lacked authority to terminate TPS because the statute that created the TPS program in 1990 referred ​only to the attorney general as the official who had authority to extend and terminate the deportation protections.

The DHS was established later, in 2002, after the September 11 attacks.

Most of the justice department’s immigration-related functions were transferred to it at that time. Saris, who was appointed by Bill Clinton, concluded Congress had likewise transferred authority over TPS to the DHS.

Since 2001, TPS holders have paid $7.8bn annually in taxes and contributed $262bn to the US economy, according to the advocacy organization Fwd.us. Many TPS holders are employed in critical industries already facing worker shortages across the country, including construction, hospitality and healthcare.

Losing TPS can leave immigrants without legal status vulnerable to arrest, detention and deportation, even with pending asylum or green card applications.

Some may face immigration court proceedings with limited options to stay in the US. People ordered removed could be deported and barred from returning for years.

Reuters contributed reporting

world.title: Ebola virus behind massive outbreak in DRC could be mutating, officials say
world.snippet: Cases have passed 4,000 and health watchdog plans to go door to door to find patients in major response escalation The virus causing a ma...
world.content:
The virus causing a massive outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo could be mutating, health officials fear, as confirmed cases pass 4,000.

Africa’s public health watchdog said the time for incremental action was over as they announced plans to scale up every aspect of the response and go “door to door” looking for patients.

The Ebola outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, was first reported on 15 May, although there are suspicions the disease could have been spreading since January.

There have been 3,973 cases and 1,801 deaths recorded as of 4 August, according to the DRC’s national public health institute. Speaking on Thursday, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), told a press briefing cases had topped 4,000.

The outbreak is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record. There are eight times more cases, and six times more deaths than were recorded 11 weeks into the West Africa Ebola outbreak in 2014-18, which infected more than 28,000 people and killed at least 11,000.

Kaseya said he had spoken to the director general of the World Health Organization, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, and they planned studies “to check if there is no additional issue, or maybe if the virus is not mutating. Because the level of severity of this Bundibugyo outbreak is unprecedented.”

More than two-thirds of Ebola deaths are happening in the community rather than in treatment centres. In a treatment centre run by MSF in Bunia, the capital of Ituri province, 90% of admitted patients do not appear on authorities’ lists of contacts of known cases. Both factors indicate high levels of untracked transmission.

Kaseya said contact tracing in the DRC was insufficient, with only 10 contacts identified for every Ebola patient, when about 40 would be the expected number.

Ebola is a viral haemorrhagic fever that can cause vomiting, diarrhoea, organ damage and internal bleeding. The outbreak is centred on the conflict-affected mining province of Ituri, but has spread to Nord-Kivu, Sud-Kivu, Haut-Uele and Tshopo. There were 20 cases recorded in neighbouring Uganda before it brought its outbreak under control.

Dr Wessam Mankoula, acting head of emergency preparedness and response at Africa CDC, said response teams planned a shift “from contact tracing to active case search”, which would mean community health workers “moving from door to door” asking households if they had anyone sick with Ebola symptoms.

He added: “I think the time for incremental action is over and we’re starting now the phase for scaling up.”

Kaseya promised a “village-centered response” that would involve communities, more use of digital tools and greater action in the camps for people who have been internally displaced by conflict in affected provinces.

Officials also said they planned to begin using antiviral remdesivir on a compassionate use basis to treat patients. They will also start testing whether Ervebo, a vaccine licensed for use against a different strain of Ebola, should be offered in the affected province, after receiving data suggesting that Bundibugyo caused less serious disease and “zero death” among people who had received that jab.

“Seeing the expansion of this outbreak, only the public health measure will not be enough to quickly control or stop this outbreak,” said Dr Placide Mbala Kingebeni, Africa CDC director of research, clinical trials and innovation.

DRC authorities said they were investigating a suspected Ebola death on a boat heading to the capital, Kinshasa, from the north-east of the country, and that the other passengers on board would be quarantined and tested.

Unicef warned that essential healthcare was being disrupted by the outbreak as fear of infection and service disruptions kept families away from clinics. In the outbreak’s centre, the mining town of Mongbwalu, the proportion of children receiving their first measles dose has fallen 69%.

world.title: US to shut five consulates as critics fear China could fill diplomatic vacuum
world.snippet: State department informs Congress of planned closures in Canada, Grenada, Japan, Indonesia and Cameroon The US state department is to shu...
world.content:
The US state department is to shut five foreign consulates and missions across Asia, Africa, North America and the Caribbean, drawing criticism that it is leaving a diplomatic vacuum at risk of being filled by China.

The US Congress has been served notice of the impending closures, which are being justified on cost grounds and follow a reassessment of the US’s bilateral relationships with a range of countries since Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.

According to a notice served to several congressional committees, missions will close in St George’s, Grenada; Nagoya, Japan; Medan, Indonesia; Douala, Cameroon; and Winnipeg, Canada.

The closures will continue a process of cutbacks in US state department operations overseen by Marco Rubio, the secretary of state. Last year, the department fired more than 1,300 employees, including 246 foreign services officers and 1,107 civil servants.

More than half of the US’s 195 ambassadorial posts around the world remain unfilled, including in keys locations such as Germany, Cuba, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, according to the American Foreign Service Association.

Democrats have criticized the latest planned closures, saying it risked leaving the field free for China.

“China has a diplomatic presence in three of the five locations where the state department is closing shop and Beijing is going to exploit that new vacuum to undercut American interests,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate foreign relations committee.

“The yearly operating costs of these diplomatic facilities represent a tiny fraction of the state department’s yearly budget,” Shaheen added. “Is that worth pulling back from these places where China is present?”

The decision to close the consulate in Winnipeg has come in for criticism in Canada, on which Trump recently announced the imposition of 50% tariffs on a range of goods.

Opened in 2001, the Winnipeg consulate has served to facilitate trade and investment issues mainly relating to the province of Manitoba, of which Winnipeg is the capital.

Brad Kirbyson, a former political specialist who worked at the consulate for 20 years, told the Canadian broadcaster CBC the closure could harm US interests.

“I’m sure it’ll save them a few dollars, but I think the net effect is to lose touch with a broad swath of Canada by not having a presence there,” he said. “The United States found that it was a very long way between the US consulate in Calgary and the [one] in Toronto.

“It makes a lot of sense to have a consulate in the middle of the country that can cover issues in this part of the world.”

A spokesperson for the Canadian embassy in Washington said: “Canada and the US have a long history of collaboration on areas of shared interest, including through our foreign offices in both countries.”

China does not have a diplomatic mission in Winnipeg, but it has a presence in St George’s, Nagoya and Medan. The US mission in St George’s, the capital of the Caribbean island of Grenada, has full embassy status, while the Douala facility is defined as an “embassy branch office”.

A state department spokesperson said: “The department is committed to following congressional notification procedures including post closures. We have nothing further to report at this time.

“We are focused on ensuring our diplomatic footprint is efficient, effective and delivers results for the American people.”

In a later statement, issued after this story was first published, a department spokesperson countered the assertion that the closures would benefit China.

“Claims that China is filling a diplomatic vacuum is [sic] inherently false and we recommend that individuals who subscribe to this propaganda take a look at the so-called help China had in the recent earthquakes in Venezuela or to address the Ebola outbreak,” the spokesperson said.

The White House’s office of management and budget has argued for a much more extensive closure program of up to 30 foreign missions.

Democrats, supported by national security and foreign policy specialists, have countered that such moves will dangerously reduce the US’s diplomatic footprint and global influence, especially when combined with last year’s dismantling of USAID, the main overseas development body, which was drastically reduced in size before being bundled into the state department.

world.title: Top Ugandan footballer killed by robbers armed with paving stones
world.snippet: David Owori, who played for the national team, died in hospital after he tried to stop robbers taking his phone The Ugandan football comm...
world.content:
The Ugandan football community is in mourning after the death of a player who was fatally injured during a robbery in the capital, Kampala, on Tuesday night.

David Owori, who captained Sports Club Villa, a Uganda Premier League club, and represented the national team, was attacked after resisting an attempt to steal his mobile phone and other belongings near his home in Makindye division.

Racheal Kawala, a spokesperson for the Kampala Metropolitan police, said he was found unconscious by ​passersby, who took him to a nearby hospital. He was ​transferred to another hospital, where he was pronounced dead on Wednesday.

Witnesses said attackers hit the footballer with paving stones before robbing him and fleeing, leaving him unconscious, the BBC reported.

Owori, 27, was a right-back and midfielder for SC Villa. He helped the team win a record 17th Uganda Premier League title in 2024.

He started his senior career in 2016 at the Uganda Premier League side Vipers Sports Club and had stints in Europe with Vélez CF in Spain and Utsiktens BK in Sweden.

He played for the national team in the qualifiers for the 2021 Africa Cup of Nations.

SC Villa said: “It is with profound sorrow that we announce the untimely passing of our captain, Owori, who had been receiving treatment at Case Clinic following an attack by suspected thugs. Our deepest condolences and prayers are with his family.”

The Federation ​of Uganda Football Associations said: “David was not just a footballer. He was ​both a leader and an inspiration to a generation. As ​Captain of SC Villa, he led with courage, humility and passion. In the Uganda Cranes jersey, he carried the hopes of a nation.”

It added: “We have lost a son, a leader and a star. His light on and off the pitch will never be forgotten.”

The Ugandan parliament observed a minute of silence in Owori’s honour on Wednesday.

In June Sydney Gongodyo, a Ugandan rugby international, ​died after a mob attacked him in Kampala, mistaking him for a thief, police said.

Uganda’s National Council of Sports said: “Sadly, ​Ugandan sport has been hit with many such ​tragedies lately, and we hope for justice and a lasting solution.”
